name: Fear of Crime: Which Street Feels Safer? (Seoul)
description: Method replication: same task and design as the paper; the images are not the paper's stimuli (new Google Street View views of the same district, © Google). Kim, Choi & Kang (2026, ISPRS IJGI 15:18) mapped perceived fear of crime in Yeongdeungpo-gu, Seoul. Participants saw two street views side by side and chose the scene that looked safer from crime-related risk, judging only from what they saw; "crime" meant interpersonal crime (assault, robbery, harassment), not traffic or natural hazards, and an "Equal" answer was allowed. 65 participants (balanced across 20s, 30s–40s and 50+) gave 178,750 answers on 20,886 Kakao Map views taken in four directions (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°, pitch 0°) at stratified sample points. Analysis as in the paper: drop Equal answers, turn the wins into a score per image (the paper trained a Swin Transformer with a RankNet loss; TrueSkill or Bradley–Terry scores serve the same purpose for a small set), then relate scores to segmentation classes and map them; the paper used SHAP to explain the model. Differences from the original study: (1) images are 67 Google Street View views (mostly 2018, a few 2009–2014) at random points in Yeongdeungpo-gu, each facing one random cardinal direction; the paper used Kakao Map 2021–2022 views and also Anyang City; (2) each participant makes 30 comparisons; the paper's question set was algorithmically balanced over thousands of comparisons per person; (3) the paper inserted five trap pairs with obvious differences to screen inattentive answers; this template has none, so add your own check if needed; (4) the age and gender questions are additions that allow the paper's group comparisons.
author: Kim, Choi & Kang
